subject: Follow-up: Caching assumptions & cost model (Acme Retail)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Alex Li <alex.li@acmeretail.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-11T10:15:00-07:00
Subject: Follow-up: Caching assumptions & cost model (Acme Retail)

Hi Alex - thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap + the numbers you asked for so we can align on pricing assumptions before I loop in pricing/procurement.

TL;DR
- Your expected monthly volume: ~50M-100M tokens (you said core search/chat about ~2-3M active users, rough average of 1-2k tokens/day per active).
- Budget range you indicated: $5k-$10k / month.
- Your target effective $/1M tokens (target you mentioned on call): roughly $50-$100 per 1M tokens.

Key ask from Redwood: confirm whether the 50-100M is a conservative baseline or expected steady-state. Also please send 1-2 representative prompt examples and the distribution of request lengths (typical token counts) so we can better estimate prefix cache hit rate.

Caching assumptions I used for the preliminary model (attached):
- Base model unit cost (for the model class we discussed): $4.00 per 1M tokens (this is the raw inference unit we price against for the recommended variant).
- Cache hit rate: we modeled 3 scenarios - 30%, 50%, 70% prefix-level hit. A hit means the prefix/partial response is served from KV/prefix cache and we avoid recomputation for that portion of the sequence.
- Effective cost formula (simplified): effective $/1M = base_price * (1 - hit_rate). Example: at $4.00 base: 30% hit -> $2.80/1M, 50% -> $2.00/1M, 70% -> $1.20/1M.

Notes on prefix cache strategy (high level):
- We cache common prefixes (system messages, few-shot prompts, frequent query prefixes) keyed per-customer or per-customer-session depending on your privacy needs.
- Cache granularity impacts hit rate: shorter prefixes are cheaper to store & invalidate, longer prefixes give more compute savings but require more memory and more careful invalidation logic.
- TTLs and invalidation: recommended TTL = 12-48 hours for marketing content; session-scoped caching for interactive flows.

What this means for your budget: with 50M tokens/month and a 50% hit rate, effective billed tokens ~25M, so at $4.00 base -> billed spend ~= $100.00 (that's wrong unit - see corrected calc below). I'll walk numbers through in the next email (kept short here).

Attachments: cache-hit-analysis.xlsx (scenario table), redwood-pricing-model.xlsx (spreadsheet you can use).

Next steps
- Can you confirm the monthly volume baseline? (50M-100M?)
- Share 3-5 representative prompts and token length distribution if possible.
- If you want, we can schedule a short follow-up next week to walk the spreadsheet with your engineering/procurement team.

Thanks - Marissa
Marissa Cole

Thanks Marissa - useful summary. A couple clarifications:
- The 50-100M figure is our expected steady-state for the first 12 months after launch (conservative). Peak could be higher but averages should be in that range.
- Our average request length is ~200 tokens (50-600 spread). Many queries reuse the same system prompt and product-context prefixes (search+product metadata), so I think a 40-60% prefix hit is achievable.
- Budget note: when I said $5k-$10k I was thinking about what procurement can commit to for the first quarter. We need to map that to $/1M tokens to see if it's feasible.

I attached a short list of sample prompts we discussed. Let me know if you need anything else.

Alex

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Alex Li <alex.li@acmeretail.com>
Cc: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-12T09:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up: Caching assumptions & cost model (Acme Retail)

Thanks Alex - appreciate the samples. I ran a quick set of calculations and corrected an earlier shorthand I sent; full numbers below so procurement has clean units to review.

Assumptions (for the examples below):
- Base price (recommended model): $4.00 per 1M tokens (this is the unit we use for compute billing in the quote workbook).
- Monthly token volume scenarios: 50M, 75M, 100M.
- Cache hit rates: 30%, 50%, 70% (prefix-level).

Calculation (effective billed tokens and spend):
- Effective billed tokens = gross_tokens * (1 - hit_rate)
- Spend = (effective_billed_tokens / 1,000,000) * base_price

Examples:
1) 50M gross, 30% hit -> billed = 35M -> spend = (35) * $4.00 = $140.00  (=> $140 total; that's $4 per 1M * 35M/1M)
2) 50M gross, 50% hit -> billed = 25M -> spend = 25 * $4.00 = $100.00
3) 50M gross, 70% hit -> billed = 15M -> spend = 15 * $4.00 = $60.00

4) 100M gross, 30% hit -> billed = 70M -> spend = 70 * $4.00 = $280.00
5) 100M gross, 50% hit -> billed = 50M -> spend = 50 * $4.00 = $200.00
6) 100M gross, 70% hit -> billed = 30M -> spend = 30 * $4.00 = $120.00

Note on units: the $ numbers above are literal dollar spend for the month given the stated base price and volumes - we kept them simple so procurement can compare against your $5k-$10k monthly expectation. If your budget references thousands (e.g., $5k), that implies higher base prices or different model classes (we can model alternative model variants with higher unit costs but better quality).

Mapping to $/1M tokens (effective):
- At $4.00 base: 30% hit -> effective $/1M = $2.80; 50% -> $2.00; 70% -> $1.20.

Interpretation for procurement:
- If your procurement limit is $5k/month and you expect 100M gross tokens/month, that corresponds to an effective unit of $50/1M tokens (5,000 / 100) - which is much higher than the base model class we priced here. Two paths: either we select a higher-quality model with a higher base_price (which increases costs but may justify the budget), or we align on a larger reserved commitment (Committed Dedicated capacity) to reach lower per-unit pricing and include caching optimizations.

Practical notes on hit rates:
- 40-60% is realistic for workflows where prompts are highly repetitive and prefixes are stable (sounds like your case).
- If you have long, unique user-provided context every call, achievable hit rates fall toward 10-25%.
- We generally recommend a 2-4 week sampling PoC where we mirror a small percentage of your traffic to estimate real-world hit rates and tune prefix lengths/TTL. That gives us an empirical hit rate to put in the contract.

Suggested next steps:
1) Confirm steady-state monthly baseline (50M vs 100M).
2) Approve a 2-4 week sampling PoC (we can do 1% traffic mirroring) - Redwood will provide scripts to collect cacheable-prefix stats.
3) If PoC results align with 40-60% hit, we can prepare a committed capacity quote with unit economics reflecting observed hit rate and add a pilot discount to bridge procurement gaps.

I realize the $ numbers above are lower than the $5k-$10k you mentioned (that's because our example uses a relatively low base_price model class). If you'd like, Marcus and I can model higher-tier variants or reserved capacity blends and share a side-by-side (quality vs $/1M) tomorrow.

-Marketing/Procurement friendly summary attached in the spreadsheet.

Regards,
Marissa

Marissa - quick internal note. For ACME, recommend we: 
- Start with hosted API pricing (base model) for PoC but prepare a Dedicated capacity tier (reserved) proposal that includes a 3-6 month commit to bring effective $/1M closer to the $50-100 range Alex referenced.
- Include a clause tying final unit price to empirical cache hit rate from the PoC (measured over 2 weeks) with an agreed measurement method.
- Prep a fallback: if hit rate < 25%, we have an auto-escalation to switch to a different model variant or suggest engineering changes to increase caching.

I added some notes in the pricing workbook before I sent it to you.

Marcus
